extracted.intended_audience: journalists, researchers, policymakers, and general readers interested in media manipulation and public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for recognizing and assessing astroturfing campaigns across online and offline media, covering definitions, legal/regulatory tests, technical detection methods, operational signals, and illustrative case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of astroturfing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Astroturfing is the deceptive practice of hiding the sponsors of an orchestrated message or organization to make it appear as though it originates from, and is supported by, unsolicited grassroots participants."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to give statements or organizations credibility by withholding information about the source's financial backers; implies a fake or artificial appearance of support. On the internet, astroturfers may use software or multiple personas to hide identity and simulate widespread support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-science framing: manufactured public consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: In political science, astroturfing is defined as the process of seeking electoral victory or legislative relief by helping political actors find and mobilize a sympathetic public, and is designed to create the image of public consensus where there is none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on campaigns designed to influence public opinion, typically funded by corporations and political entities rather than spontaneously arising from constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC endorsement/testimonial rules (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Trade Commission's 'Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising' (updated in 2009) holds advertisers responsible for ensuring bloggers or product endorsers comply and requires disclosure when there is a material connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC may issue cease-and-desist orders or fines (noted example: $16,000 per day). Guides apply to social media and word-of-mouth marketing; advertisers can be held liable for undisclosed paid endorsements or reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unfair Commercial Practices Directive requires that paid-for editorial content in the media provide a clear disclosure that the content is a sponsored advertisement and prohibits misleading readers into thinking a promoter is a regular consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to paid editorial content; material connections must be disclosed to avoid misleading consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits 'Falsely representing oneself as a consumer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations can carry up to two years in prison and unlimited fines. The advertising industry also uses voluntary codes (e.g., Code of Non-Broadcast Advertising) that require marketers not to mislead audiences, including by omitting disclosure of material connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian Consumer Law — misleading or deceptive conduct (s18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 broadly prohibits 'misleading and deceptive conduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Australian enforcement is often via competitor lawsuits rather than regulator action; language is broader/vaguer than some other regimes, so outcomes depend on litigation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal target: testimonials, endorsements, and declarations of performance/quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal regulations are primarily targeted towards testimonials, endorsements and statements as to the performance or quality of a product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees of an organization may be treated as customers if their actions are not guided by authority within the company; failure to disclose material connections to sponsors can trigger regulatory or civil actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques indicating astroturfing (operational/behavioral signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common techniques include use of front groups, fake blogs presented as consumer-written, incentivized form letters, mass letters printed in multiple newspapers, fake/paid reviewers, sockpuppets (multiple identities operated by one person), persona-management software, and persona ageing/automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeated identical letters, personalized stationery that is mass-produced, multiple accounts with similar behavior, coordinated timing of posts, paid-poster business models, and use of software to manage many convincing personas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection methods (technical research approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers use content analysis, linguistic analysis, authorship attribution, machine learning, and behavioral-pattern recognition to detect astroturfing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include software that recognizes behavioral patterns on Twitter, identification via profile-image reuse, timing and volume analysis (high-volume posting), and machine-learning classifiers trained on coordinated activity features. Detection methods continually evolve as operatives adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/market indicators of astroturfing services
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial indicators include explicit pricing models (e.g., grass-roots specialists charging $25–$75 per constituent; paid online commentators paid per post; companies selling batches of fake reviews for fixed prices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of paid-for posts, documented pricing, or business operations advertising review/letter-writing services is a strong indicator of inauthentic campaigning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persona and account-management artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Persona-management software can age accounts, simulate conference attendance, and enable each paid poster to manage multiple convincing online identities without confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical artifacts include account aging patterns, simultaneous or near-simultaneous activity across many accounts, identical or similar visual cues and account setup, and evidence of coordinated account handbooks or tools (e.g., thumb drives with account credentials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-media trend manipulation indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Astroturfing targets platform features used as popularity proxies (e.g., Twitter trends) by coordinating fake/compromised accounts to tweet in a coordinated way to mimic grassroots organizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited (e.g., EPFL) found a measurable fraction of global Twitter trends were artificial. Rapid, coordinated spikes from similar accounts, duplication of meme text or hashtags, and bot-like posting schedules are signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness and failure conditions (evaluation of impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Astroturfing can alter public viewpoints, create uncertainty, lower trust, and sway discussions through groupthink — but elite-sponsored campaigns often fail if not transparent about sponsorship or if they do not build genuine constituency partnerships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical studies and case histories to assess whether the campaign produced measurable opinion change or merely created noise; transparency and authentic constituency ties are key moderators of success/failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented legal and enforcement examples as evidentiary criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete enforcement actions (e.g., Entergy fined $5 million for hiring actors; New York Attorney General settlements with companies for fake reviews) are direct proof of illegal astroturfing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite settlements, fines, and official findings when assessing a suspected campaign; these examples also show which behaviors regulators prioritize (fake reviews, paid actors, undeclared sponsored content).

rubrics_metrics.name: State-sponsored and foreign-influence indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: State actors may run coordinated astroturfing operations at scale (e.g., allegations of hundreds of thousands of government employees posting propaganda; military persona-management solicitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals include large networks of duplicate or linked accounts, cross-border advertising spend tied to political topics, and patterns of content that systematically favor a state's narratives; platform enforcement removals (pages/accounts) are further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and societal impact criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Astroturfing threatens the legitimacy of genuine grassroots movements, undermines public ability to assess product claims or public policy, and represents an ethical lapse when designed to manipulate opinion or harm research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should consider effects on civic discourse, consumer protection, and research integrity; calls for stronger regulatory or policy responses are common where harms are documented.
